content: The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management: Guidelines on Good Labeling Practice for Pesticides (Revised) was published in August 2015 by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations and the World Health Organization (WHO). This document provides comprehensive guidance on pesticide labeling to ensure safety, compliance, and effective communication of essential information to users. The guidelines emphasize that reproduction and dissemination of the material for educational or non-commercial purposes are permitted without prior written permission, provided the source is fully acknowledged. However, reproduction for resale or commercial purposes is prohibited without written consent from the copyright holders. The FAO and WHO have taken all reasonable precautions to verify the accuracy of the information in this publication. However, the material is distributed without any warranty, expressed or implied. The responsibility for interpreting and using the material lies with the reader, and neither FAO nor WHO shall be held liable for any damages arising from its use. The document reflects the collective views of an international group of experts and does not necessarily represent the official policies or decisions of FAO or WHO. It includes definitions of key terms such as active ingredient, co-formulant, hazard statement, and precautionary statement, among others, to ensure clarity and consistency in pesticide labeling practices. The guidelines trace the evolution of pesticide labeling standards, starting with the FAO's initial publication in 1985, followed by revisions in 1988 and 1995. Significant developments in pesticide and chemical management, including the adoption of the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labeling of Chemicals (GHS) in 2003, have influenced these guidelines. The revised version aligns with the GHS and provides specific options for pesticide labeling where national interpretation of GHS provisions is allowed. The document is structured into six chapters, covering objectives, GHS introduction, required label information, label design and content, hazard and risk classifications, and the importance of information provision and training. Annexes include examples of label statements, hazard color bands, and precautionary pictograms to aid in understanding and implementation. The guidelines are primarily intended for pesticide regulatory authorities, particularly in developing countries and economies in transition, to help define or revise national pesticide labeling requirements. They also assist pesticide registration authorities in reviewing draft labels. Other stakeholders, such as the pesticide industry and civil society groups, may find the guidelines useful for drafting or evaluating pesticide labels. The pesticide label is defined as a mandatory part of the product package, providing essential use recommendations, safety information, and hazard warnings. It serves as the primary communication tool between manufacturers and users, helping to protect human health and the environment. In many countries, pesticide labels are legal documents, and their content and format are regulated by law. Any modifications to labels must be approved by the responsible authority, and using a pesticide in a manner inconsistent with its labeling is considered a violation. The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management outlines responsibilities for governments and the pesticide industry regarding labeling. The pesticide industry is expected to ensure proper labeling of products sold and distributed nationally and internationally, particularly in countries without established regulatory frameworks.
